claim: Pitch perception is critical for recognizing speech, music and animal vocalizations.
source: Pitch perception is critical for recognizing speech, music and animal vocalizations, but its neurobiological basis remains unsettled, in part because of divergent results across species.
evidence: This is a general statement about the importance of pitch perception, supported by established scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: The neurobiological basis of pitch perception remains unsettled, in part because of divergent results across species.
source: Pitch perception is critical for recognizing speech, music and animal vocalizations, but its neurobiological basis remains unsettled, in part because of divergent results across species.
evidence: This statement reflects the current state of scientific understanding and is based on inference from the literature.

claim: Ferrets accurately generalized pitch discriminations to untrained stimuli whenever temporal envelope cues were robust in the probe sounds.
source: Ferrets accurately generalized pitch discriminations to untrained stimuli whenever temporal envelope cues were robust in the probe sounds, but not when resolved harmonics were the main available cue.
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically the results shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Ferrets did not accurately generalize pitch discriminations to untrained stimuli when resolved harmonics were the main available cue.
source: Ferrets accurately generalized pitch discriminations to untrained stimuli whenever temporal envelope cues were robust in the probe sounds, but not when resolved harmonics were the main available cue.
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral experimental data presented in the manuscript, specifically the results shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Human listeners exhibited the opposite pattern of results on an analogous task compared to ferrets, consistent with previous studies.
source: By contrast, human listeners exhibited the opposite pattern of results on an analogous task, consistent with previous studies.
evidence: This claim is supported by the behavioral experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figure 5B) and references to previous studies.

claim: Differences in the relative salience of the two pitch cues can be attributed to differences in cochlear filter bandwidths between ferrets and humans.
source: Simulated cochlear responses in the two species suggest that differences in the relative salience of the two pitch cues can be attributed to differences in cochlear filter bandwidths.
evidence: This claim is supported by the computational modeling results presented in Figure 1 and the comparison with behavioral data.

claim: Cross-species variation in pitch perception reflects the constraints of estimating a sound's fundamental frequency given species-specific cochlear tuning.
source: The results support the view that cross-species variation in pitch perception reflects the constraints of estimating a sound's fundamental frequency given species-specific cochlear tuning.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the integration of modeling and behavioral data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The way that F0 changes encodes meaning in speech.
source: The way that F0 changes encodes meaning in speech (Ohala, 1983) and musical melody (Cousineau et al., 2009; Dowling and Fujitani, 1971; Krumhansl, 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ohala, 1983.

claim: The way that F0 changes encodes musical melody.
source: The way that F0 changes encodes meaning in speech (Ohala, 1983) and musical melody (Cousineau et al., 2009; Dowling and Fujitani, 1971; Krumhansl, 1990).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cousineau et al., 2009; Dowling and Fujitani, 1971; Krumhansl, 1990.

claim: The F0 of a person's voice provides a cue to their identity.
source: The F0 of a person's voice provides a cue to their identity (Gelfer and Mikos, 2005; Latinus and Belin, 2011; McPherson and McDermott, 2018) and helps us attend to them in a noisy environment (Darwin, 2005; Miller et al., 2010; Popham et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gelfer and Mikos, 2005; Latinus and Belin, 2011; McPherson and McDermott, 2018.

claim: The F0 of a person's voice helps us attend to them in a noisy environment.
source: The F0 of a person's voice provides a cue to their identity (Gelfer and Mikos, 2005; Latinus and Belin, 2011; McPherson and McDermott, 2018) and helps us attend to them in a noisy environment (Darwin, 2005; Miller et al., 2010; Popham et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Darwin, 2005; Miller et al., 2010; Popham et al., 2018.

claim: Pitch is believed to help non-human animals identify individuals and interpret communication calls.
source: The vocal calls of non-human animals are also often periodic, and pitch is believed to help them to identify individuals and interpret communication calls (Koda and Masataka, 2002; Nelson, 1989).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Koda and Masataka, 2002; Nelson, 1989.

claim: Many mammalian species have been shown to discriminate the F0 of periodic sounds in experimental settings.
source: Many mammalian species have been shown to discriminate the F0 of periodic sounds in experimental settings (Heffner and Whitfield, 1976; Osmanski et al., 2013; Shofner et al., 2007; Tomlinson and Schwarz, 1988; Walker et al., 2009), and these animal models hold promise for understanding the neural mechanisms that underlie pitch perception.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Heffner and Whitfield, 1976; Osmanski et al., 2013; Shofner et al., 2007; Tomlinson and Schwarz, 1988; Walker et al., 2009.

claim: Pitch acuity can differ markedly across species.
source: However, pitch acuity can differ markedly across species (Shofner, 2005; Walker et al., 2009), raising the possibility that humans and other mammals may use different neural mechanisms to extract pitch.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Shofner, 2005; Walker et al., 2009.

claim: The auditory cortex plays a key role in pitch processing.
source: The auditory cortex plays a key role in pitch processing, but it remains unclear how cortical neurons extract the F0 of a sound (Wang and Walker, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wang and Walker, 2012.

claim: It remains unclear how cortical neurons extract the F0 of a sound.
source: The auditory cortex plays a key role in pitch processing, but it remains unclear how cortical neurons extract the F0 of a sound (Wang and Walker, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Wang and Walker, 2012 and reflects current scientific understanding.

claim: Neural correlates of F0 cues have been observed across auditory cortical fields in some species.
source: Neural correlates of F0 cues (Bendor and Wang, 2010; Bizley et al., 2009; Fishman et al., 2013) and pitch judgments (Bizley et al., 2013) have been observed across auditory cortical fields in some species, while specialized 'pitch-tuned' neurons have thus far only been described in marmoset auditory cortex (Bendor and Wang, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bendor and Wang, 2010; Bizley et al., 2009; Fishman et al., 2013.

claim: Neural correlates of pitch judgments have been observed across auditory cortical fields in some species.
source: Neural correlates of F0 cues (Bendor and Wang, 2010; Bizley et al., 2009; Fishman et al., 2013) and pitch judgments (Bizley et al., 2013) have been observed across auditory cortical fields in some species, while specialized 'pitch-tuned' neurons have thus far only been described in marmoset auditory cortex (Bendor and Wang, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bizley et al., 2013.

claim: Specialized 'pitch-tuned' neurons have thus far only been described in marmoset auditory cortex.
source: Neural correlates of F0 cues (Bendor and Wang, 2010; Bizley et al., 2009; Fishman et al., 2013) and pitch judgments (Bizley et al., 2013) have been observed across auditory cortical fields in some species, while specialized 'pitch-tuned' neurons have thus far only been described in marmoset auditory cortex (Bendor and Wang, 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Bendor and Wang, 2005.

claim: There is a lack of consensus regarding the neural code for pitch in the human brain.
source: There is a similar lack of consensus regarding the neural code for pitch in the human brain (Griffiths and Hall, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Griffiths and Hall, 2012.

claim: Pitch discrimination in humans is thought to be driven by two acoustical cues that result from low-numbered 'resolved' harmonics and high-numbered 'unresolved' harmonics.
source: Pitch discrimination in humans is thought to be driven by two acoustical cues that result from low-numbered 'resolved' harmonics and high-numbered 'unresolved' harmonics (Moore and Gockel, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Moore and Gockel, 2011.

claim: In the frequency domain, F0 can be determined from the distribution of harmonics.
source: In the frequency domain, F0 can be determined from the distribution of harmonics (Figure 1A, upper panel) (Goldstein, 1973; Shamma and Klein, 2000; Terhardt, 1974).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Goldstein, 1973; Shamma and Klein, 2000; Terhardt, 1974, and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: In the auditory nerve, the frequency spectrum is represented as a 'place code' of activation across the tonotopic map as well as a 'temporal code' of spikes that are phase-locked to basilar membrane vibrations.
source: In the auditory nerve, the frequency spectrum is represented as a 'place code' of activation across the tonotopic map as well as a 'temporal code' of spikes that are phase-locked to basilar membrane vibrations (Cariani and Delgutte, 1996; Schnupp et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cariani and Delgutte, 1996; Schnupp et al., 2011.

claim: Both place code and temporal code representations are limited by the cochlea's frequency resolution.
source: However, both these representations are limited by the cochlea's frequency resolution (Goldstein, 1973).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Goldstein, 1973.

claim: Cochlear filter bandwidths increase with frequency.
source: Because cochlear filter bandwidths increase with frequency, only low-numbered harmonics produce discernible peaks of excitation and phase locked spikes at their centre frequency (Figure 1A, middle panel).
evidence: This is established knowledge in auditory science, illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Only low-numbered harmonics produce discernible peaks of excitation and phase locked spikes at their centre frequency.
source: Because cochlear filter bandwidths increase with frequency, only low-numbered harmonics produce discernible peaks of excitation and phase locked spikes at their centre frequency (Figure 1A, middle panel).
evidence: This claim is based on established knowledge and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: High-numbered harmonics produce beating in time at the F0, conveyed by phase-locking to their envelope.
source: By contrast, high-numbered harmonics are not individually resolved, and instead produce beating in time at the F0, conveyed by phase-locking to their envelope (Schouten, 1970) (Figure 1A, bottom panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Schouten, 1970 and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Humans can extract F0 using either resolved harmonics or unresolved harmonics alone.
source: Although psychophysical experiments have demonstrated that humans can extract F0 using either resolved harmonics or unresolved harmonics alone (Bernstein and Oxenham, 2003; Houtsma and Smurzynski, 1990; Shackleton and Carlyon, 1994), human pitch perception is generally dominated by resolved harmonics (Ritsma, 1967; Shackleton and Carlyon, 1994; Shofner and Campbell, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bernstein and Oxenham, 2003; Houtsma and Smurzynski, 1990; Shackleton and Carlyon, 1994.

claim: Human pitch perception is generally dominated by resolved harmonics.
source: Although psychophysical experiments have demonstrated that humans can extract F0 using either resolved harmonics or unresolved harmonics alone (Bernstein and Oxenham, 2003; Houtsma and Smurzynski, 1990; Shackleton and Carlyon, 1994), human pitch perception is generally dominated by resolved harmonics (Ritsma, 1967; Shackleton and Carlyon, 1994; Shofner and Campbell, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ritsma, 1967; Shackleton and Carlyon, 1994; Shofner and Campbell, 2012.

claim: Marmosets can use resolved harmonics to detect F0 changes.
source: Marmosets can also use resolved harmonics to detect F0 changes (Bendor et al., 2012; Song et al., 2016), whereas rodents (i.e. gerbils and chinchillas) rely more upon temporal periodicity cues (Klinge and Klump, 2010; Klinge and Klump, 2009; Shofner and Chaney, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bendor et al., 2012; Song et al., 2016.

claim: Rodents (i.e. gerbils and chinchillas) rely more upon temporal periodicity cues.
source: Marmosets can also use resolved harmonics to detect F0 changes (Bendor et al., 2012; Song et al., 2016), whereas rodents (i.e. gerbils and chinchillas) rely more upon temporal periodicity cues (Klinge and Klump, 2010; Klinge and Klump, 2009; Shofner and Chaney, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Klinge and Klump, 2010; Klinge and Klump, 2009; Shofner and Chaney, 2013.

claim: Species differences in perception could relate to the pitch cues that are available following cochlear filtering.
source: It has been suggested that these apparent species differences in perception could relate to the pitch cues that are available following cochlear filtering (Cedolin and Delgutte, 2010; Shofner and Chaney, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cedolin and Delgutte, 2010; Shofner and Chaney, 2013.

claim: Cochlear bandwidths are broader in many non-human species.
source: In particular, the growing evidence that cochlear bandwidths are broader in many non-human species (Joris et al., 2011; Shera et al., 2002), including ferrets (Alves-Pinto et al., 2016; Sumner et al., 2018), supports the possibility that they might process pitch cues in different ways from humans, as has been noted previously (Shofner and Campbell, 2012; Shofner and Chaney, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Joris et al., 2011; Shera et al., 2002.

claim: Ferrets have broader cochlear bandwidths than humans.
source: In particular, the growing evidence that cochlear bandwidths are broader in many non-human species (Joris et al., 2011; Shera et al., 2002), including ferrets (Alves-Pinto et al., 2016; Sumner et al., 2018), supports the possibility that they might process pitch cues in different ways from humans, as has been noted previously (Shofner and Campbell, 2012; Shofner and Chaney, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Alves-Pinto et al., 2016; Sumner et al., 2018.

claim: The spectral range of stimuli was not fully controlled across F0 in some previous studies.
source: Second, the spectral range of stimuli was not fully controlled across F0 in some previous studies (e.g. Song et al., 2016; Walker et al., 2009), making it possible for animals to base their behavioural choices on the lower spectral edge of the sounds, rather than the sound's overall F0.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Song et al., 2016; Walker et al., 2009.

claim: The pitch difference thresholds of ferrets can differ by orders of magnitude between a go/no-go and 2AFC task.
source: For example, the pitch difference thresholds of ferrets can differ by orders of magnitude between a go/no-go and 2AFC task (Walker et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Walker et al., 2011.

claim: Humans are believed to have narrower cochlear filter bandwidths than ferrets.
source: Humans (Glasberg and Moore, 1990; Shera et al., 2002) are believed to have narrower cochlear filter bandwidths than ferrets (Alves-Pinto et al., 2016; Sumner et al., 2018; Sumner and Palmer, 2012) and other non-human animals (Joris et al., 2011; Osmanski et al., 2013; Pickles and Comis, 1976), and these physiological constraints may predispose them to rely on different acoustical cues to classify the pitch of complex tones.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Glasberg and Moore, 1990; Shera et al., 2002 for humans and Alves-Pinto et al., 2016; Sumner et al., 2018; Sumner and Palmer, 2012 for ferrets.

claim: Sharper frequency tuning in humans should result in more resolvable harmonics across the human tonotopic map.
source: Specifically, sharper frequency tuning in humans should result in more resolvable harmonics across the human tonotopic map.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between cochlear filter bandwidth and harmonic resolvability.

claim: Broader bandwidth of an auditory nerve fibre should result in stronger phase locking to the beating of adjacent harmonics.
source: On the other hand, if the bandwidth of an auditory nerve fibre is broader, its firing should phase lock more strongly to the beating of adjacent harmonics, potentially providing a stronger explicit representation of the temporal periodicity of F0 in ferrets than in humans.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between cochlear filter bandwidth and temporal envelope representation.

claim: The cochlear filters are wider for the ferret auditory nerve than the human.
source: As shown in Figure 1B, the cochlear filters are wider for the ferret auditory nerve than the human, even with the difference in the methods used to obtain the two sets of bandwidth estimates.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Individual low-numbered harmonics of the tone are more clearly resolved in the human cochlea than in the ferret.
source: When the instantaneous power of the cochlear filters is summed across the duration of the sound and plotted as a function of centre frequency, the individual low-numbered harmonics of the tone are more clearly resolved in the human cochlea than in the ferret (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: The representation of the 500 Hz F0 is clearer in the ferret than in the human in the temporal domain.
source: To visualize the temporal representation of the higher harmonics in the same stimulus, we plotted the output of a single nerve fibre (here, a fibre with a centre frequency of 5 kHz) throughout time (Figure 1D). In this case, the representation of the 500 Hz F0 is clearer in the ferret – the human cochlea produces weaker temporal modulation because fewer harmonics fall within the fibre's bandwidth.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: The average temporal representation of F0 was enhanced in the ferret compared to the human.
source: The average temporal representation of F0 was enhanced in the ferret compared to the human (Wilcoxon rank sum test; z = 8.286, p=1.175×10−16).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the cochlear model data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: The F0 representation metric was higher in the ferret than the human cochlear model across every pair of individually simulated auditory nerve fibres.
source: In fact, this F0 representation metric was higher in the ferret than the human cochlear model across every pair of individually simulated auditory nerve fibres.
evidence: This claim is supported by the cochlear model data.

claim: The ferret cochlea provides an enhanced representation of the envelope periodicity of a complex tone, as conveyed by spikes that are phase-locked to the F0 in the auditory nerve.
source: These simulations suggest that the ferret cochlea provides an enhanced representation of the envelope periodicity of a complex tone, as conveyed by spikes that are phase-locked to the F0 in the auditory nerve.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cochlear model simulations.

claim: The human auditory nerve provides a better resolved representation of individual harmonics across the tonotopic array.
source: On the other hand, the human auditory nerve provides a better resolved representation of individual harmonics across the tonotopic array.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cochlear model simulations.

claim: Five ferrets were trained on a two-alternative forced choice (2AFC) task that requires 'low' and 'high' pitch judgements.
source: To test the role of different pitch cues in ferret pitch perception, we trained five animals on a two-alternative forced choice (2AFC) task that requires 'low' and 'high' pitch judgements analogous to those used in human psychophysical tasks (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Four ferrets were trained to classify harmonic complex tones with an F0 of 500 and 1000 Hz.
source: We began by training four ferrets to classify harmonic complex tones with an F0 of 500 and 1000 Hz, with a repeating pure tone presented at 707 Hz (the midpoint on a logarithmic scale) for reference before each trial.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: Three ferrets were trained to classify harmonic complex tones with target F0 values of 150 and 450 Hz.
source: Two of these animals, along with one naïve ferret, were then trained on the same task using target F0 values of 150 and 450 Hz and a 260 Hz pure tone reference.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods used in the study.

claim: The integer ratios between the F0s to be discriminated allowed exact matching of their spectral bandwidths.
source: In both cases, the integer ratios between the F0s to be discriminated allowed us to match their spectral bandwidths exactly, so that ferrets could not solve the task based on the frequency range of the sound (Figure 3; first four rows).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design rationale.

claim: The ferrets learned to perform the pitch classification task within 22 ± 3 days of twice daily training.
source: After completing several pre-training stages to habituate the animals to the apparatus and sound presentation (see Materials and methods), the ferrets learned to perform the pitch classification task within 22 ± 3 (mean ± standard deviation) days of twice daily training.
evidence: This is a report of experimental results.

claim: The inner ear produces distortion in response to harmonic tones that can introduce energy at the fundamental frequency to the basilar membrane response.
source: The inner ear is known to produce distortion in response to harmonic tones that can introduce energy at the fundamental frequency to the basilar membrane response, even for missing-fundamental sounds (Robles et al., 1991).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Robles et al., 1991.

claim: Ferrets performed more poorly on probe trials than on standard trials.
source: Ferrets performed more poorly on probe trials than on standard trials (paired t-test; t = 4.346, p=0.005), as expected for an auditory discrimination task performed in noise.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: Ferrets performed the pitch classification at 71.85 ± 9.60% correct with the noise masker.
source: However, they performed the pitch classification at 71.85 ± 9.60% correct (mean ± standard deviation) with the noise masker, which is well above chance (1-sample t-test; t = 6.025, p=0.001).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: Ferrets did not rely on cochlear distortion products to solve the pitch classification task.
source: This suggests that ferrets did not rely on cochlear distortion products to solve our task.
evidence: This is an inference based on the behavioral data showing above-chance performance with noise masking.

claim: The standard tones contained both resolved and unresolved harmonics for ferret listeners.
source: This analysis suggests that our standard tones contained both resolved and unresolved harmonics for ferret listeners, as intended.
evidence: This is an inference based on the auditory nerve model analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Performance varied with stimulus type (i.e., the standard and four probe stimuli).
source: A repeated-measures 3-way ANOVA was carried out on the three ferrets trained with both references. This analysis indicated that performance varied with stimulus type (i.e., the standard and four probe stimuli) (F(4,8) = 10.540, p=0.003), but not across subjects (F(2,8) = 1.060; p=0.391) or the two reference conditions (i.e., 260 and 707 Hz) (F(1,8) = 0.438, p=0.576).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: Ferret performance did not vary across subjects.
source: A repeated-measures 3-way ANOVA was carried out on the three ferrets trained with both references. This analysis indicated that performance varied with stimulus type (i.e., the standard and four probe stimuli) (F(4,8) = 10.540, p=0.003), but not across subjects (F(2,8) = 1.060; p=0.391) or the two reference conditions (i.e., 260 and 707 Hz) (F(1,8) = 0.438, p=0.576).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: Ferret performance did not vary across the two reference conditions (i.e., 260 and 707 Hz).
source: A repeated-measures 3-way ANOVA was carried out on the three ferrets trained with both references. This analysis indicated that performance varied with stimulus type (i.e., the standard and four probe stimuli) (F(4,8) = 10.540, p=0.003), but not across subjects (F(2,8) = 1.060; p=0.391) or the two reference conditions (i.e., 260 and 707 Hz) (F(1,8) = 0.438, p=0.576).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: Compared to their performance on standard trials, ferrets showed impaired performance on probes that contained only low harmonics.
source: To assess the acoustical cues used by animals to solve the pitch classification task, we compared ferrets' performance on the standard trials with that on each of the four probe trial types (repeated measures 2-way ANOVA, Tukey's HSD test). Compared to their performance on standard trials, ferrets showed impaired performance on probes that contained only low harmonics (p=0.001), but performed well when only high harmonics were presented (p=1.000).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: Ferrets performed well when only high harmonics were presented.
source: To assess the acoustical cues used by animals to solve the pitch classification task, we compared ferrets' performance on the standard trials with that on each of the four probe trial types (repeated measures 2-way ANOVA, Tukey's HSD test). Compared to their performance on standard trials, ferrets showed impaired performance on probes that contained only low harmonics (p=0.001), but performed well when only high harmonics were presented (p=1.000).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: Ferrets' performance was impaired when the phases of the high harmonics were randomized.
source: Their performance was impaired when we randomized the phases of the high harmonics (p=0.002).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: Phase randomization impaired ferret performance when the full set of harmonics (both resolved and unresolved; 'All Harmonics Random Phase') were present.
source: Phase randomization also impaired performance when the full set of harmonics (both resolved and unresolved; 'All Harmonics Random Phase') were present (p=2.173×10−5).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: Ferrets rely more strongly on the temporal envelope periodicity (produced by unresolved harmonics) than on resolved harmonics to classify the pitch of harmonic tone complexes.
source: This pattern of results suggests that ferrets rely more strongly on the temporal envelope periodicity (produced by unresolved harmonics) than on resolved harmonics to classify the pitch of harmonic tone complexes, unlike what would be expected for human listeners.
evidence: This is an inference based on the pattern of behavioral results.

claim: Human listeners showed varied pitch classification performance across the standard and probe stimuli.
source: Human listeners also showed varied pitch classification performance across the standard and probe stimuli (repeated-measures 2-way ANOVA; F(4,60) = 36.999, p=1.443×10−15).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: A different pattern of performance across stimuli was observed for human subjects than for ferrets.
source: However, a different pattern of performance across stimuli was observed for human subjects than for ferrets (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of the behavioral data shown in Figure 5A and 5B.

claim: Human listeners were significantly impaired when resolved harmonics were removed from the sounds.
source: Tukey's HSD tests indicated that human listeners were significantly impaired when resolved harmonics were removed from the sounds, as demonstrated by impairments in the 'High Harmonic' probes with (p=9.922×10−9) and without (p=1.029×10−8) randomized phases.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: No impairment was observed in human listeners when resolved harmonics were available, regardless of whether the phases of stimuli were randomized or not.
source: Conversely, no impairment was observed when resolved harmonics were available, regardless of whether the phases of stimuli were randomized ('All Harmonics Random Phase' condition; p=0.959) or not ('Low Harmonics' condition; p=0.101).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: While ferrets were impaired only when temporal envelope cues from unresolved harmonics were disrupted, humans continued to classify the target pitch well in the absence of temporal envelope cues, so long as resolved harmonics were present.
source: Consistent with the relative prominence of the cues in our model simulations, we found that while ferrets were impaired only when temporal envelope cues from unresolved harmonics were disrupted, humans continued to classify the target pitch well in the absence of temporal envelope cues, so long as resolved harmonics were present.
evidence: This is a summary of the behavioral results comparing the two species.

claim: There was a significant interaction between species and stimulus type on performance.
source: This was confirmed statistically as a significant interaction between species and stimulus type on performance (2-way ANOVA; F(4,135) = 14.720, p=5.274×10−10).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the behavioral data.

claim: The two species predominantly rely on distinct cues to pitch.
source: The two species thus appear to predominantly rely on distinct cues to pitch.
evidence: This is an inference based on the behavioral results.

claim: Broader cochlear filter widths in ferrets result in fewer resolved harmonics and a more enhanced representation of temporal envelopes than the human cochlea.
source: Our model simulations illustrated how broader cochlear filter widths in ferrets result in fewer resolved harmonics and a more enhanced representation of temporal envelopes than the human cochlea, as suggested by previous authors (Cedolin and Delgutte, 2010; Shofner and Chaney, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cochlear model simulations and citations to previous work.

claim: The results provide the first unambiguous dissociation of pitch mechanisms across species.
source: Our results provide the first unambiguous dissociation of pitch mechanisms across species, by utilizing the same task across species, and provide an illustration of the potential consequences of species differences in cochlear tuning.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim about the significance of the study's findings.

claim: Human listeners have consistently been found to have better pitch discrimination thresholds when stimuli contain resolved harmonics.
source: Human listeners have consistently been found to have better pitch discrimination thresholds when stimuli contain resolved harmonics (Bernstein and Oxenham, 2003; Kaernbach and Bering, 2001; Moore et al., 1985; Ritsma, 1967; Shackleton and Carlyon, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bernstein and Oxenham, 2003; Kaernbach and Bering, 2001; Moore et al., 1985; Ritsma, 1967; Shackleton and Carlyon, 1994.

claim: Cortical responses to pitched sound in humans are stronger for resolved than unresolved harmonics, mirroring perceptual sensitivity.
source: Moreover, cortical responses to pitched sound in humans are stronger for resolved than unresolved harmonics, mirroring perceptual sensitivity (Norman-Haignere et al., 2013; Penagos et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Norman-Haignere et al., 2013; Penagos et al., 2004.

claim: Humans may learn to derive pitch primarily from resolved harmonics even when temporal envelope cues are also available.
source: Because most natural sounds contain both low- and high-numbered harmonics, humans may learn to derive pitch primarily from resolved harmonics even when temporal envelope cues are also available, and are thus less equipped to derive pitch from unresolved harmonics alone.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed behavioral pattern.

claim: Ferrets may learn to rely more on temporal pitch cues when estimating pitch from natural sounds.
source: As a result, they may conversely learn to rely more on temporal pitch cues when estimating pitch from natural sounds, leading to poorer performance for low harmonic tone complexes.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed behavioral pattern in ferrets.

claim: Species differences in pitch perception may be even more pronounced than suggested by the simulations.
source: In fact, these species differences may be even more pronounced than suggested by our simulations, as ferret filters appear to exhibit broader bandwidths when measured with the simultaneous masking paradigms from which the human bandwidths in our simulations were obtained (Sumner et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on citation to Sumner et al., 2018.

claim: Many non-human mammals are thought to have wider cochlear bandwidths than humans.
source: Many non-human mammals are thought to have wider cochlear bandwidths than humans (Joris et al., 2011; Liberman, 1978; Sumner et al., 2018; Temchin et al., 2008), and so we might expect temporal cues to dominate their pitch decisions as we have observed in ferrets.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Joris et al., 2011; Liberman, 1978; Sumner et al., 2018; Temchin et al., 2008.

claim: Studies in gerbils suggest that they primarily use temporal cues to detect an inharmonic component in a tone complex.
source: For instance, studies in gerbils suggest that they primarily use temporal cues to detect an inharmonic component in a tone complex (Klinge and Klump, 2010; Klinge and Klump, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Klinge and Klump, 2010; Klinge and Klump, 2009.

claim: Chinchillas were shown to detect the onset of a periodic sound following a non-periodic sound using temporal, rather than resolved harmonic, cues.
source: Chinchillas were similarly shown to detect the onset of a periodic sound following a non-periodic sound using temporal, rather than resolved harmonic, cues (Shofner, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Shofner, 2002.

claim: Marmosets appear to be influenced by harmonic phases when detecting changes in F0 only when resolved harmonics are omitted from the stimulus.
source: Marmosets, on the other hand, appear to be influenced by harmonic phases when detecting changes in F0 only when resolved harmonics are omitted from the stimulus (Bendor et al., 2012; Osmanski et al., 2013; Song et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bendor et al., 2012; Osmanski et al., 2013; Song et al., 2016.

claim: Temporal cues are only salient for marmosets when they occur in unresolved harmonics.
source: This suggests that temporal cues are only salient for this species when they occur in unresolved harmonics.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited marmoset studies.

claim: Marmosets were found to detect smaller changes in F0 when harmonics were resolved than when only unresolved harmonics were available.
source: Similarly to humans, marmosets were found to detect smaller changes in F0 when harmonics were resolved than when only unresolved harmonics were available (Song et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Song et al., 2016.

claim: Ferrets show an order of magnitude difference in pitch acuity on F0 change detection versus F0 direction labeling tasks.
source: Ferrets show an order of magnitude difference in pitch acuity on these two tasks (Walker et al., 2011), raising the possibility that primates might as well.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Walker et al., 2011.

claim: The results do not preclude the possibility that ferrets could also make pitch judgments based on resolved harmonics if trained to do so.
source: The ferrets relied predominantly on temporal cues under these conditions, but our results do not preclude the possibility that they could also make pitch judgments based on resolved harmonics if trained to do so.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the limitations of the study's conclusions.

claim: Humans can extract pitch from unresolved harmonics when they are isolated.
source: Indeed, although human listeners rely on resolved harmonics under normal listening conditions, we can also extract pitch from unresolved harmonics when they are isolated (Moore et al., 1985; Ritsma, 1967; Shackleton and Carlyon, 1994).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Moore et al., 1985; Ritsma, 1967; Shackleton and Carlyon, 1994.

claim: Multiple harmonics could potentially be resolved on the ferret cochlea, depending on the F0.
source: Our simulations show that multiple harmonics could potentially be resolved on the ferret cochlea, depending on the F0 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by the cochlear model simulations shown in Figure 4A.

claim: If specifically trained to do so, one might expect ferrets to be able to derive F0 from resolved harmonics using the same template matching mechanisms proposed for human listeners.
source: Consequently, if specifically trained to do so, one might expect ferrets to be able to derive F0 from these harmonics using the same template matching mechanisms proposed for human listeners (Goldstein, 1973; Shamma and Klein, 2000).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the modeling results and citations to Goldstein, 1973; Shamma and Klein, 2000.

claim: The relationship between harmonic resolvability and auditory nerve tuning is not fully understood.
source: As discussed above, it is also important to note that the relationship between harmonic resolvability and auditory nerve tuning is not fully understood, and nonlinearities in response to multiple frequency components could cause resolvability to be worse than that inferred from isolated auditory nerve fibre measurements.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of current scientific knowledge.

claim: Pitch judgments are adapted to the acoustical cues that are available and robust in a particular species.
source: Overall, the available evidence fits with the idea that pitch judgments are adapted to the acoustical cues that are available and robust in a particular species, with differences in cochlear tuning thus producing cross-species diversity in pitch perception.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim synthesizing the study's findings.

claim: Listeners appear to rely on harmonicity for some pitch tasks and spectral changes in others, potentially because of task-dependent differences in the utility of particular cues.
source: A similar principle may be at work within human hearing, where listeners appear to rely on harmonicity for some pitch tasks and spectral changes in others, potentially because of task-dependent differences in the utility of particular cues (McPherson and McDermott, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to McPherson and McDermott, 2018.

claim: Ferrets can estimate F0 from the temporal envelopes of harmonic complex tones.
source: The present experiments suggest that ferrets, a common animal model in studies of hearing (e.g. Atilgan et al., 2018; Bizley et al., 2013; Fritz et al., 2003; Schwartz and David, 2018), can estimate F0 from the temporal envelopes of harmonic complex tones.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the behavioral data.

claim: Ferrets generalize across sounds with different spectral properties without relying on explicit energy at the F0.
source: Our data indicate that ferrets generalize across sounds with different spectral properties (including wideband sounds, sounds in noise, and sounds containing only high harmonics) without relying on explicit energy at the F0.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the behavioral data.

claim: Ferrets appear to have a pitch percept, even though the cues underlying it are apparently weighted differently than in human pitch perception.
source: In this respect, ferrets appear to have a pitch percept, even though the cues underlying it are apparently weighted differently than in human pitch perception.
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the behavioral results.

claim: Ferrets appear to favour temporal cues over resolved harmonic cues even for F0s as high as 1000 Hz.
source: It is interesting that ferrets appear to favour temporal cues over resolved harmonic cues even for F0s as high as 1000 Hz.
evidence: This is an observation based on the behavioral data.

claim: 1000 Hz falls above a reported temporal pitch limit in cats and humans.
source: While this periodicity is well below the phase locking limit of the ferret auditory nerve (Sumner and Palmer, 2012), it falls above a reported temporal pitch limit in cats (Chung and Colavita, 1976) and humans (Carlyon and Deeks, 2002; Macherey and Carlyon, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chung and Colavita, 1976 for cats and Carlyon and Deeks, 2002; Macherey and Carlyon, 2014 for humans.

claim: Ferrets were possibly performing the 707 Hz reference task by detecting the absence of temporal modulation at 1000 Hz.
source: We thus cannot rule out the possibility that ferrets were actually performing the 707 Hz reference task by detecting the absence of temporal modulation at 1000 Hz.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation for the behavioral results.

claim: The similar pattern of performance for the lower pair of reference F0s (150 and 450 Hz) supports the idea that the ferrets were basing their judgments on temporal pitch cues.
source: However, the similar pattern of performance for the lower pair of reference F0s (150 and 450 Hz) is less plausibly explained in this way, and supports the idea that the ferrets were basing their judgments on temporal pitch cues.
evidence: This is an inference based on the behavioral data.

claim: It is possible that the temporal modulation limit of pitch is higher in an animal that relies more on this cue.
source: It is also possible that the temporal modulation limit of pitch is higher in an animal that relies more on this cue.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis.

claim: Primates are more appropriate animal models for examining the role of resolved harmonics in human pitch perception.
source: The existing literature might be taken to suggest that primates are more appropriate animal models for examining the role of resolved harmonics in human pitch perception, as they appear to be more like humans in their use of this cue (Bendor et al., 2012; Osmanski et al., 2013; Song et al., 2016).
evidence: This is an inference based on citations to Bendor et al., 2012; Osmanski et al., 2013; Song et al., 2016.

claim: Ferrets are a powerful animal model for evaluating temporal models of pitch extraction.
source: On the other hand, our data suggest that ferrets are a powerful animal model for evaluating temporal models of pitch extraction (e.g. Meddis et al., 1997).
evidence: This is an interpretive claim based on the study's findings and a citation to Meddis et al., 1997.

claim: Like cochlear implant users, ferrets have broad cochlear frequency filters that may limit their use of resolved harmonic cues.
source: Like cochlear implant users, ferrets have broad cochlear frequency filters that may limit their use of resolved harmonic cues.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cochlear modeling results and comparison to cochlear implant users.

claim: Five adult female pigmented ferrets (aged 6–24 months) were trained in this study.
source: Five adult female pigmented ferrets (aged 6–24 months) were trained in this study.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: The pitch classification performance of 16 adult humans (nine male, ages 18–53 years; mean age = 25.3 years) was examined.
source: The pitch classification performance of 16 adult humans (nine male, ages 18–53 years; mean age = 25.3 years) was also examined, which provided a 60% beta in the power calculations described for ferrets.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: All human subjects reported having normal hearing.
source: All subjects reported having normal hearing.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental subjects.

claim: Ferrets ran two training sessions daily, and typically completed 94 ± 24 trials per session.
source: Ferrets ran two training sessions daily, and typically completed 94 ± 24 trials per session (mean ± standard deviation).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: The water reward presented from the peripheral response spouts (0.3–0.5 ml per trial) was larger than that presented at the central start spout (0.1–0.2 ml per trial).
source: The water reward presented from the peripheral response spouts (0.3–0.5 ml per trial) was larger than that presented at the central start spout (0.1–0.2 ml per trial).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: The animal was required to remain in the central nose poke for 300 ms to receive a water reward from that spout.
source: The animal was required to remain in the central nose poke for 300 ms to receive a water reward from that spout.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: The reference pure tone's frequency was set to halfway between the low and high target F0s on a log scale.
source: The reference pure tone's frequency was set to halfway between the low and high target F0s on a log scale.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: The 150 and 450 Hz targets were chosen to overlap with the F0 range that was tested in human listeners.
source: The 150 and 450 Hz targets were chosen to overlap with the F0 range that we tested in human listeners (below).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design rationale.

claim: The 500 and 1000 Hz condition was included as ferrets often perform better on pitch discrimination tasks in this range than on sounds with lower F0s.
source: The 500 and 1000 Hz condition was included as ferrets often perform better on pitch discrimination tasks in this range than on sounds with lower F0s (Walker et al., 2009).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design rationale supported by a citation to Walker et al., 2009.

claim: The level of the noise masker was set so that the power at the output of a Gammatone filter centred at the F0 was 5 dB below the level of the pure tone components of the target.
source: The level of the noise masker was set so that the power at the output of a Gammatone filter centred at the F0 (with bandwidth matched to ferret auditory nerve measurements in that range [Sumner and Palmer, 2012]) was 5 dB below the level of the pure tone components of the target.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Distortion products are expected to be at least 15 dB below the level of the stimulus components based on measurements in humans.
source: This is conservative because distortion products are expected to be at least 15 dB below the level of the stimulus components based on measurements in humans (Norman-Haignere and McDermott, 2016; Pressnitzer and Patterson, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Norman-Haignere and McDermott, 2016; Pressnitzer and Patterson, 2001.

claim: The number of resolved harmonics was approximated as the ratio of F0 and the bandwidth of auditory nerve fibres with a characteristic frequency at that F0.
source: For a given F0, the number of resolved harmonics was approximated as the ratio of F0 and the bandwidth of auditory nerve fibres with a characteristic frequency at that F0, as described by Moore and Ohgushi (1993), and applied by Osmanski et al. (2013).
evidence: This is a description of the analysis method supported by citations to Moore and Ohgushi, 1993 and Osmanski et al., 2013.

claim: This measure yielded between 1 and 8 resolved harmonics for ferrets, depending on the F0.
source: This measure yielded between 1 and 8 resolved harmonics for ferrets, depending on the F0 (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is a result of the analysis shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Human listeners were tested on a pitch classification task that was designed to be as similar as possible to Stage 3 of ferrets' task.
source: Human subjects were tested on a pitch classification task that was designed to be as similar as possible to Stage 3 of ferrets' task (see above).
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: 16 human subjects discriminated target F0s of 180 and 220 Hz.
source: 16 subjects discriminated target F0s of 180 and 220 Hz.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental methods.

claim: Due to the smaller F0 difference required to make the task difficult enough to challenge human listeners, it was not possible to match the lower spectral edge of the 'Low Harmonic' and 'All Harmonic' stimuli as was done for ferrets.
source: Due to the smaller F0 difference required to make the task difficult enough to challenge human listeners (Walker et al., 2009), it was not possible to match the lower spectral edge of the 'Low Harmonic' and 'All Harmonic' stimuli as we did for ferrets.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design constraints supported by a citation to Walker et al., 2009.

claim: The stimuli were set such that the higher F0 target had the lower spectral edge.
source: However, the stimuli were set such that the higher F0 target had the lower spectral edge.
evidence: This is a description of the experimental design.

claim: Because feedback was not provided for probe trials, it is unlikely that human subjects could have learned to associate a lower spectral edge with the higher F0.
source: Because feedback was not provided, it is unlikely that subjects could have learned to associate a lower spectral edge with the higher F0 and vice versa.
evidence: This is an inference about the experimental design.

claim: Error correction trials were excluded from all data analysis.
source: Error correction trials were excluded from all data analysis, as were data from any testing session in which the subject scored less than 60% correct on standard trials.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methods.

claim: Data from any testing session in which the subject scored less than 60% correct on standard trials were excluded from analysis.
source: Error correction trials were excluded from all data analysis, as were data from any testing session in which the subject scored less than 60% correct on standard trials.
evidence: This is a description of the data analysis methods.
